You are implementing ONE requirement in the Apache Hadoop source tree at /workspace (a real upstream repo checked out at an earlier state).

REQUIREMENT SLUG: unixshellguide-typo
REQUIREMENT FILE: /workspace/requirements/unixshellguide-typo.yaml   <-- READ THIS FIRST

The `title:` field names the real upstream Apache Hadoop JIRA / git commit. Your job is to reproduce that upstream change as faithfully as you can from the requirement text plus the code you find in the tree. Hidden tests derived from the real upstream commit will grade the result, so EXACT naming matters:
  * new/changed configuration keys and their default values (and their entries in *-default.xml)
  * new class / interface / method / field / metric names and their visibility
  * log message wording and format placeholders
  * behavioural details (return values, exception types, ordering, off-by-one boundaries)
If the requirement text names an identifier (class, method, config key, metric, constant), use that identifier verbatim.

HOW TO WORK
1. Read the requirement yaml. Note the JIRA id and the module it belongs to (HDFS / YARN / MAPREDUCE / HADOOP-common / tools).
2. Locate the real code with Grep/Glob. Read enough surrounding code (and the existing tests for it) to make a correct, idiomatic change.
3. Implement the change. Match the surrounding code style, license headers, checkstyle habits (2-space indent, 80-col-ish, final where used, LOG placeholders `{}`).
4. If the change adds a config key, also add it to the matching `*-default.xml` (hdfs-default.xml / core-default.xml / yarn-default.xml / mapred-default.xml) with a sensible description, and to the `DFSConfigKeys`/`YarnConfiguration`/etc. constants class the module uses. Some modules have a TestYarnConfigurationFields / TestHdfsConfigFields style test that requires the xml and the constant to agree - keep them in sync.
5. If the upstream change would have come with tests, add or extend the corresponding test class under the same module (src/test/java/...). Keep tests deterministic and cheap. Do not add tests that need network or a real cluster beyond the usual MiniDFSCluster/MiniYARNCluster idioms already used in that test file.
6. Do NOT run maven/mvn or cmake (there is no warm build environment; it wastes your time). Instead be rigorous by inspection: every symbol you reference must exist (grep to confirm), every new import must be needed and correct, braces/parens balanced, no stale references left behind. Re-read your own final diff (`git diff -- <your files>`) before finishing and fix anything sloppy.
7. Scope discipline: change ONLY what this requirement needs. Do not reformat unrelated lines, do not fix unrelated warnings, do not touch other subsystems. Other agents are concurrently implementing ~380 other requirements in this same working tree.

FORBIDDEN COMMANDS (they would destroy other agents' concurrent work): git checkout / switch / stash / reset / revert / clean / rebase / merge / cherry-pick, `git add -A` or `git add .` without an explicit pathspec, `git commit --amend`, `git rm` of files you did not create, and any `mvn`/`gradle` invocation.

WHEN YOUR IMPLEMENTATION IS COMPLETE - commit it yourself with exactly this shape (substitute the real repo-relative paths you touched, space separated, and keep the flock):

  cd /workspace && flock /tmp/hadoop-git.lock bash -c 'git add -A -- PATH1 PATH2 ... && git diff --cached --binary > requirement_patches/unixshellguide-typo.diff && git commit -q -m "impl: unixshellguide-typo" && git log --oneline -1 && wc -c requirement_patches/unixshellguide-typo.diff'

Rules for that step:
  * List every file you created, modified or deleted as an explicit pathspec. Never a bare directory like `.`.
  * requirement_patches/unixshellguide-typo.diff MUST come out non-empty (wc -c > 0). If `git commit` reports "nothing to commit", another agent already committed your lines: verify the requirement is genuinely satisfied in the working tree, then report that in your notes.
  * Do not touch requirement_patches/ for any other slug.

FINALLY return ONLY a JSON object (this is your return value, not a message to a human):
{"slug":"unixshellguide-typo","status":"done"|"partial"|"blocked","files":["..."],"committed":true|false,"patch_bytes":<int>,"summary":"<=3 sentences on what you changed","notes":"anything the orchestrator must know (conflicts, follow-ups, uncertainty)"}

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

1	title: HADOOP-17564. Fix typo in UnixShellGuide.html
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Developers reading Hadoop''s Unix shell guide use it as reference material while wiring scripts and environment settings. Even a minor typo in that guide can make the documentation look less trustworthy than it should.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  The Unix shell guide should correct the affected typo while leaving the guidance and shell behavior unchanged. This is a documentation cleanup only.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  The typo in the Unix shell guide is corrected, the surrounding documentation remains intact, and no shell functionality or configuration behavior changes.
16	
17	  '
18

1	<!---

4	  You may obtain a copy of the License at

9	  distributed under the License is distributed on an "AS IS" BASIS,
10	  WITHOUT WARRANTIES OR CONDITIONS OF ANY KIND, either express or implied.
11	  See the License for the specific language governing permissions and
12	  limitations under the License. See accompanying LICENSE file.
13	-->
14	
15	# Unix Shell Guide
16	
17	<!-- MACRO{toc|fromDepth=0|toDepth=3} -->
18	
19	Much of Apache Hadoop's functionality is controlled via [the shell](CommandsManual.html).  There are several ways to modify the default behavior of how these commands execute.
20	
21	## Important End-User Environment Variables
22	
23	Apache Hadoop has many environment variables that control various aspects of the software.  (See `hadoop-env.sh` and related files.)  Some of these environment variables are dedicated to helping end users manage their runtime.
24	
25	### `HADOOP_CLIENT_OPTS`
26	
27	This environment variable is used for all end-user, non-daemon operations.  It can be used to set any Java options as well as any Apache Hadoop options via a system property definition. For example:
28	
29	```bash
30	HADOOP_CLIENT_OPTS="-Xmx1g -Dhadoop.socks.server=localhost:4000" hadoop fs -ls /tmp
31	```
32	
33	will increase the memory and send this command via a SOCKS proxy server.
34	
35	NOTE: If 'YARN_CLIENT_OPTS' is defined, it will replace 'HADOOP_CLIENT_OPTS' when commands are run with 'yarn'.
36	
37	### `(command)_(subcommand)_OPTS`
38	
39	It is also possible to set options on a per subcommand basis.  This allows for one to create special options for particular cases.  The first part of the pattern is the command being used, but all uppercase.  The second part of the command is the subcommand being used.  Then finally followed by the string `_OPT`.
40	
41	For example, to configure `mapred distcp` to use a 2GB heap, one would use:
42	
43	```bash
44	MAPRED_DISTCP_OPTS="-Xmx2g"
45	```
46	
47	These options will appear *after* `HADOOP_CLIENT_OPTS` during execution and will generally take precedence.
48	
49	### `HADOOP_CLASSPATH`
50	
51	  NOTE: Site-wide settings should be configured via a shellprofile entry and permanent user-wide settings should be configured via ${HOME}/.hadooprc using the `hadoop_add_classpath` function. See below for more information.
52	
53	The Apache Hadoop scripts have the capability to inject more content into the classpath of the running command by setting this environment variable.  It should be a colon delimited list of directories, files, or wildcard locations.
54	
55	```bash
56	HADOOP_CLASSPATH=${HOME}/lib/myjars/*.jar hadoop classpath
57	```
58	
59	A user can provides hints to the location of the paths via the `HADOOP_USER_CLASSPATH_FIRST` variable.  Setting this to any value will tell the system to try and push these paths near the front.
60	
61	### Auto-setting of Variables
62	
63	If a user has a common set of settings, they can be put into the `${HOME}/.hadoop-env` file.  This file is always read to initialize and override any variables that the user may want to customize.  It uses bash syntax, similar to the `.bashrc` file:
64	
65	For example:
66	
67	```bash
68	#
69	# my custom Apache Hadoop settings!
70	#
71	
72	HADOOP_CLIENT_OPTS="-Xmx1g"
73	MAPRED_DISTCP_OPTS="-Xmx2g"
74	HADOOP_DISTCP_OPTS="-Xmx2g"
75	```
76	
77	The `.hadoop-env` file can also be used to extend functionality and teach Apache Hadoop new tricks.  For example, to run hadoop commands accessing the server referenced in the environment variable `${HADOOP_SERVER}`, the following in the `.hadoop-env` will do just that:
78	
79	```bash
80	
81	if [[ -n ${HADOOP_SERVER} ]]; then
82	  HADOOP_CONF_DIR=/etc/hadoop.${HADOOP_SERVER}
83	fi
84	```
85	
86	One word of warning:  not all of Unix Shell API routines are available or work correctly in `.hadoop-env`.  See below for more information on `.hadooprc`.
87	
88	## Administrator Environment
89	
90	In addition to the various XML files, there are two key capabilities for administrators to configure Apache Hadoop when using the Unix Shell:
91	
92	  * Many environment variables that impact how the system operates.  This guide will only highlight some key ones.  There is generally more information in the various `*-env.sh` files.
93	
94	  * Supplement or do some platform-specific changes to the existing scripts.  Apache Hadoop provides the capabilities to do function overrides so that the existing code base may be changed in place without all of that work.  Replacing functions is covered later under the Shell API documentation.
95	
96	### `(command)_(subcommand)_OPTS`
97	
98	By far, the most important are the series of `_OPTS` variables that control how daemons work.  These variables should contain all of the relevant settings for those daemons.
99	
100	Similar to the user commands above, all daemons will honor the `(command)_(subcommand)_OPTS` pattern.  It is generally recommended that these be set in `hadoop-env.sh` to guarantee that the system will know which settings it should use on restart.  Unlike user-facing subcommands, daemons will *NOT* honor `HADOOP_CLIENT_OPTS`.
101	
102	In addition, daemons that run in an extra security mode also support `(command)_(subcommand)_SECURE_EXTRA_OPTS`.  These options are *supplemental* to the generic `*_OPTS` and will appear after, therefore generally taking precedence.
103	
104	### `(command)_(subcommand)_USER`
105	
106	Apache Hadoop provides a way to do a user check per-subcommand.  While this method is easily circumvented and should not be considered a security-feature, it does provide a mechanism by which to prevent accidents.  For example, setting `HDFS_NAMENODE_USER=hdfs` will make the `hdfs namenode` and `hdfs --daemon start namenode` commands verify that the user running the commands are the hdfs user by checking the `USER` environment variable.  This also works for non-daemons.  Setting `HADOOP_DISTCP_USER=jane` will verify that `USER` is set to `jane` before being allowed to execute the `hadoop distcp` command.
107	
108	If a \_USER environment variable exists and commands are run with a privilege (e.g., as root; see hadoop_privilege_check in the API documentation), execution will switch to the specified user first.  For commands that support user account switching for security reasons and therefore have a SECURE\_USER variable (see more below), the base \_USER variable needs to be the user that is expected to be used to switch to the SECURE\_USER account.  For example:
109	
110	```bash
111	HDFS_DATANODE_USER=root
112	HDFS_DATANODE_SECURE_USER=hdfs
113	```
114	
115	will force 'hdfs --daemon start datanode' to be root, but will eventually switch to the hdfs user after the privileged work has been completed.
116	
117	Be aware that if the \-\-workers flag is used, the user switch happens *after* ssh is invoked.  The multi-daemon start and stop commands in sbin will, however, switch (if appropriate) prior and will therefore use the keys of the specified \_USER.
118	
119	## Developer and Advanced Administrator Environment
120	
121	### Shell Profiles
122	
123	Apache Hadoop allows for third parties to easily add new features through a variety of pluggable interfaces.  This includes a shell code subsystem that makes it easy to inject the necessary content into the base installation.
124	
125	Core to this functionality is the concept of a shell profile.  Shell profiles are shell snippets that can do things such as add jars to the classpath, configure Java system properties and more.
126	
127	Shell profiles may be installed in either `${HADOOP_CONF_DIR}/shellprofile.d` or `${HADOOP_HOME}/libexec/shellprofile.d`.  Shell profiles in the `libexec` directory are part of the base installation and cannot be overridden by the user.  Shell profiles in the configuration directory may be ignored if the end user changes the configuration directory at runtime.
128	
129	An example of a shell profile is in the libexec directory.
130	
131	### Shell API
132	
133	Apache Hadoop's shell code has a [function library](./UnixShellAPI.html) that is open for administrators and developers to use to assist in their configuration and advanced feature management.  These APIs follow the standard [Apache Hadoop Interface Classification](./InterfaceClassification.html), with one addition: Replaceable.
134	
135	The shell code allows for core functions to be overridden. However, not all functions can be or are safe to be replaced.  If a function is not safe to replace, it will have an attribute of Replaceable: No.  If a function is safe to replace, it will have the attribute of Replaceable: Yes.
136	
137	In order to replace a function, create a file called `hadoop-user-functions.sh` in the `${HADOOP_CONF_DIR}` directory.  Simply define the new, replacement function in this file and the system will pick it up automatically.  There may be as many replacement functions as needed in this file.  Examples of function replacement are in the `hadoop-user-functions.sh.examples` file.
138	
139	Functions that are marked Public and Stable are safe to use in shell profiles as-is.  Other functions may change in a minor release.
140	
141	### User-level API Access
142	
143	In addition to `.hadoop-env`, which allows individual users to override `hadoop-env.sh`, user's may also use `.hadooprc`.  This is called after the Apache Hadoop shell environment has been configured and allows the full set of shell API function calls.
144	
145	For example:
146	
147	```bash
148	hadoop_add_classpath /some/path/custom.jar
149	```
150	
151	would go into `.hadooprc`
152	
153	### Dynamic Subcommands
154	
155	Utilizing the Shell API, it is possible for third parties to add their own subcommands to the primary Hadoop shell scripts (hadoop, hdfs, mapred, yarn).
156	
157	Prior to executing a subcommand, the primary scripts will check for the existence of a (scriptname)\_subcommand\_(subcommand) function.  This function gets executed with the parameters set to all remaining command line arguments.  For example, if the following function is defined:
158	
159	```bash
160	function yarn_subcommand_hello
161	{
162	  echo "$@"
163	  exit $?
164	}
165	```
166	
167	then executing `yarn --debug hello world I see you` will activate script debugging and call the `yarn_subcommand_hello` function as:
168	
169	```bash
170	yarn_subcommand_hello world I see you
171	```
172	
173	which will result in the output of:
174	
175	```bash
176	world I see you
177	```
178	
179	It is also possible to add the new subcommands to the usage output. The `hadoop_add_subcommand` function adds text to the usage output.  Utilizing the standard HADOOP\_SHELL\_EXECNAME variable, we can limit which command gets our new function.
180	
181	```bash
182	if [[ "${HADOOP_SHELL_EXECNAME}" = "yarn" ]]; then
183	  hadoop_add_subcommand "hello" client "Print some text to the screen"
184	fi
185	```
186	
187	We set the subcommand type to be "client" as there are no special restrictions, extra capabilities, etc.  This functionality may also be use to override the built-ins.  For example, defining:
188	
189	```bash
190	function hdfs_subcommand_fetchdt
191	{
192	  ...
193	}
194	```
195	
196	... will replace the existing `hdfs fetchdt` subcommand with a custom one.
197	
198	Some key environment variables for Dynamic Subcommands:
199	
200	* HADOOP\_CLASSNAME
201	
202	This is the name of the Java class to use when program execution continues.
203	
204	* HADOOP\_PRIV\_CLASSNAME
205	
206	This is the name of the Java class to use when a daemon is expected to be run in a privileged mode.  (See more below.)
207	
208	* HADOOP\_SHELL\_EXECNAME
209	
210	This is the name of the script that is being executed.  It will be one of hadoop, hdfs, mapred, or yarn.
211	
212	* HADOOP\_SUBCMD
213	
214	This is the subcommand that was passed on the command line.
215	
216	* HADOOP\_SUBCMD\_ARGS
217	
218	This array contains the argument list after the Apache Hadoop common argument processing has taken place and is the same list that is passed to the subcommand function as arguments.  For example, if `hadoop --debug subcmd 1 2 3` has been executed on the command line, then `${HADOOP_SUBCMD_ARGS[0]}` will be 1 and `hadoop_subcommand_subcmd` will also have $1 equal to 1.  This array list MAY be modified by subcommand functions to add or delete values from the argument list for further processing.
219	
220	* HADOOP\_SECURE\_CLASSNAME
221	
222	If this subcommand runs a service that supports the secure mode, this variable should be set to the classname of the secure version.
223	
224	* HADOOP\_SUBCMD\_SECURESERVICE
225	
226	Setting this to true will force the subcommand to run in secure mode regardless of hadoop\_detect\_priv\_subcmd.  It is expected that HADOOP\_SECURE\_USER will be set to the user that will be executing the final process. See more about secure mode.
227	
228	* HADOOP\_SUBCMD\_SUPPORTDAEMONIZATION
229	
230	If this command can be executed as a daemon, set this to true.
231	
232	* HADOOP\_USER\_PARAMS
233	
234	This is the full content of the command line, prior to any parsing done. It will contain flags such as `--debug`.  It MAY NOT be manipulated.
235	
236	The Apache Hadoop runtime facilities require functions exit if no further processing is required.  For example, in the hello example above, Java and other facilities were not required so a simple `exit $?` was sufficient.  However, if the function were to utilize `HADOOP_CLASSNAME`, then program execution must continue so that Java with the Apache Hadoop-specific parameters will be launched against the given Java class. Another example would be in the case of an unrecoverable error.  It is the function's responsibility to print an appropriate message (preferably using the hadoop_error API call) and exit appropriately.
237	
238	### Running with Privilege (Secure Mode)
239	
240	Some daemons, such as the DataNode and the NFS gateway, may be run in a privileged mode.  This means that they are expected to be launched as root and (by default) switched to another userid via jsvc.  This allows for these daemons to grab a low, privileged port and then drop superuser privileges during normal execution. Running with privilege is also possible for 3rd parties utilizing Dynamic Subcommands. If the following are true:
241	
242	   * (command)\_(subcommand)\_SECURE\_USER environment variable is defined and points to a valid username
243	   * HADOOP\_SECURE\_CLASSNAME is defined and points to a valid Java class
244	
245	then the shell scripts will attempt to run the class as a command with privilege as it would the built-ins.  In general, users are expected to define the \_SECURE\_USER variable and developers define the \_CLASSNAME in their shell script bootstrap.
246
